answers.label: Benefits and challenges of consequential methods
answers.text:
Consequential Accounting is how to measure real world carbon impact in the power sector. Attributional inventories, including LBM and MBM, do not measure impact. Their purpose is to accurately account for usage of clean electricity (MWhs, not MTCO2e). While this is an important foundation, we see many benefits to Consequential Accounting as a path to impactful investment in renewable energy projects. We encourage the GHGP to send the right investment signal to the market to increase market participation and accelerate decarbonization of power generation. Decision-useful data are available to guide procurement choices for the most impactful projects by accounting for the emissions impact of electricity projects.

Suggested approach:

The work of the Consequential Impacts group is critical to understanding how this type of accounting will be incorporated into the WRI protocols, but it seems to be on a different timeline. We believe that decisions related to the Consequential Electricity Sector Emissions Impact Consultation should be made in parallel with the decisions around Scope 2 Accounting so stakeholders can understand how these interrelate.
Reporting frameworks should capture real carbon reductions from PPAs in high-impact locations and create incentives that drive renewable energy growth and meaningful emissions reductions globally.

Concerns With Proposed Changes:

We understand that there is a separate Actions and Market Instruments Technical Working Group that is “…advancing work started by a subgroup of the Scope 2 TWG to further develop accounting methods for consequential actions and the Consequential Electricity Sector Emissions Impact Consultation will inform that ongoing work.” The Consequential workstream and Scope 2 work streams should be reviewed in parallel, since they interrelate.
